definition: In computer vision, the motion field is an ideal representation of motion in three-dimensional space (3D) as it is projected onto a camera image.
details: Given a simplified camera model, each point ( y 1 , y 2 ) {\displaystyle (y_{1},y_{2})} in the image is the projection of some point in the 3D scene but the position of the projection of a fixed point in space can vary with time. The motion field can formally be defined as the time derivative of the image position of all image points given that they correspond to fixed 3D points. This means that the motion field can be represented as a function which maps image coordinates to a 2-dimensional vector. The motion field is an ideal description of the projected 3D motion in the sense that it can be formally defined but in practice it is normally only possible to determine an approximation of the motion field from the image data.

explainer.lead: The motion field is the ideal projection of 3D motion onto the camera image plane. It gives the theoretical target that motion estimation and optical-flow methods try to recover.

tiers.eli5: Think of the shadow of a fly buzzing around a lamp on the wall — the motion field is the pattern of how that shadow moves as the fly moves in three dimensions.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use the motion field as the ground-truth abstraction when deriving or evaluating flow algorithms; the pitfall is that real image measurements only approximate it, since brightness changes and occlusion break the ideal correspondence.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, the motion field is the time derivative of the image position of all image points, given that they correspond to fixed 3D points; it can be represented as a function mapping image coordinates to a two-dimensional vector.

explainer.example: For a camera moving forward, the motion field for scene points points radially outward from the focus of expansion, growing in magnitude with distance from that centre.
